title: Two Circles on the Legs
statement: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezium with $AB$ parallel to $CD$. The circle with diameter $AD$ and the circle with diameter $BC$ touch each other externally at the point $P$. Given that $PA = 75$, $PD = 100$ and $PB = 65$, find $PC$.
hints: Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AD$ and $BC$. Where does $P$ lie relative to the segment $MN$, and what kind of triangle is $MAP$?

The circles touch at $P$, so $P$ lies on the segment $MN$ of centres, which is the midline of the trapezium and so is parallel to $AB$. Chase angles in the isosceles triangle $MAP$ using this parallel, and show that $AP$ bisects angle $DAB$. Then do the same at $B$, $C$ and $D$.

So $P$ is at the same distance $r$ from all four sides. As $P$ lies on both circles, the angles $APD$ and $BPC$ are right angles, so $r$ is the altitude to the hypotenuse of each of the right triangles $APD$ and $BPC$. Write $r$ in terms of $PA$ and $PD$, and also in terms of $PB$ and $PC$.
solution: Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AD$ and $BC$, the centres of the circles. As the circles touch externally at $P$, the point $P$ lies on segment $MN$, the midline of the trapezium, so $MP \parallel AB$. Since $MA = MP$, we get $\angle PAD = \angle MPA = \angle PAB$, using alternate angles for the second step. So $AP$ bisects angle $DAB$. In the same way $DP$, $BP$ and $CP$ bisect the other three angles, so $P$ is at the same distance $r$ from all four sides. Since $P$ lies on both circles, $\angle APD = \angle BPC = 90^\circ$, and $r$ is the altitude to the hypotenuse in both right triangles. From $PA \cdot PD = AD \cdot r$ and $AD^2 = PA^2 + PD^2$, $$\dfrac{1}{PA^2} + \dfrac{1}{PD^2} = \dfrac{1}{r^2} = \dfrac{1}{PB^2} + \dfrac{1}{PC^2}.$$ Here $\frac{1}{75^2} + \frac{1}{100^2} = \frac{125^2}{75^2 \cdot 100^2} = \frac{1}{60^2}$, so $r = 60$. Then $\frac{1}{PC^2} = \frac{1}{60^2} - \frac{1}{65^2} = \frac{25^2}{60^2 \cdot 65^2}$, so $PC = \frac{60 \cdot 65}{25} = 156$. Solution 2. Touching gives $MN = \frac{1}{2}(AD + BC)$, and the midline gives $MN = \frac{1}{2}(AB + CD)$, so $AB + CD = AD + BC$ and the trapezium has an inscribed circle. Its centre $I$ lies on $MN$, as it is equidistant from $AB$ and $CD$, and $\angle AID = 90^\circ$, as $AI$ and $DI$ bisect angles that add up to $180^\circ$. So $MI = \frac{1}{2}AD = MP$, giving $I = P$, and the computation above follows.

solution_figures.alt: Trapezium ABCD with AB parallel to CD. The circles on the legs AD and BC as diameters, centred at their midpoints M and N, touch at P on the midline MN. Segments PA = 75, PD = 100, PB = 65 and PC = 156 make right angles APD and BPC. A dashed circle of radius 60 centred at P touches all four sides: P is the centre of the inscribed circle.
